hints: Compare the functional groups in $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and think about gain of hydrogen versus gain of oxygen.
walkthrough:
Track what happens to the functional group**
Look closely at the change. You start with a carboxylic acid, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, and you end with a primary alcohol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The $\text{C=O}$ has become $\text{CH}_2$ and an $\text{OH}$ remains. That is a gain of hydrogen and loss of oxygen at carbon, which is reduction.

hints: Recall which reagents replace the $\text{OH}$ group of an alcohol with $\text{Cl}$ without changing the carbon skeleton.
walkthrough:
Spot the functional group swap**
You are going from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Only $\text{OH}$ is swapped for $\text{Cl}$. At AS level the classic clean reagents for this are phosphorus chlorides or thionyl chloride. Think $\text{PCl}_5$, $\text{PCl}_3$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$, all give the chloroalkane plus HCl containing byproducts.
Final answer: $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{NaCl}$ / $\text{KCl}$ with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or conc. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$

hints: Write the reactants and products for removal of $\text{HCl}$ from 1-chloropropane, remembering $\text{NaOH}$ provides $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ to form $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Recall why hot ethanolic alkali favours elimination to an alkene whereas aqueous alkali favours substitution to an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Balance the elimination equation**
Picture 1-chloropropane losing $\text{H}$ from one carbon and $\text{Cl}$ from the neighbour to form the $\text{C=C}$ in propene. The $\text{H}$ joins $\text{OH}^-$ to make $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and the $\text{Cl}$ joins $\text{Na}^+$ to make $\text{NaCl}$. So: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_6 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NaCl}$$

Choose conditions that force elimination**
$\text{NaOH}$ can act as a nucleophile in water to give substitution, or as a base in ethanol to give elimination. To get propene you need ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ with heat under reflux. Ethanol as solvent plus heating pushes the reaction down the elimination pathway.

Final answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_6 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NaCl}$
ethanolic (ethanol solvent), heat / reflux

hints: Think of the standard way to remove $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ directly from an alcohol to form an alkene using an acid catalyst or hot alumina.
walkthrough:
See this as dehydration**
Going straight from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$ is loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ across neighbouring carbons. The usual AS method is dehydration with concentrated sulfuric acid or concentrated phosphoric acid with heat, or passing vapour over heated $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.
Final answer: conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or conc. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ or $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, with heat

hints: Consider whether propene joining to itself to give poly(propene) loses any small molecule or simply adds across the $\text{C=C}$.
walkthrough:
Recognise the polymerisation type**
Propene is an alkene with a $\text{C=C}$ bond. Thousands of propene molecules simply add to each other by opening the double bond, with no other product lost. That is the definition of addition polymerisation.

hints: Start from what stays the same in stereoisomers, the order in which atoms are bonded together.
Focus on what is different, the fixed 3D arrangement in space that cannot be interchanged without breaking bonds.
walkthrough:
State what is identical**
Imagine two molecules built from exactly the same atoms joined in exactly the same order. They have the same molecular formula and the same structural formula. That is the first half of the definition.

State what is different**
Now imagine those identical connections are arranged differently in 3D space, like left and right hands or groups on opposite sides of a $\text{C=C}$. Because rotation is restricted or a chiral centre is present, the arrangements are non interconvertible. That difference in spatial arrangement completes the definition.
Final answer: Molecules with the same structural formula (same molecular formula and same connectivity) but with different three dimensional / spatial arrangement of atoms or groups.

hints: Draw propene $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_3$ adding twice so the chain becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{-}$ with continuation bonds at each end.
Look at the carbon bearing the $\text{CH}_3$ group in the polymer and list its four attached groups to test for chirality.
Recall which type of stereoisomerism requires a carbon with four different groups and rotates plane polarised light.
walkthrough:
Build two repeat units correctly**
Take $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH(CH}_3\text{)}$ and open the double bond. Each monomer becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{-}$. Join two together: $$\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{-}$$ Show $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3$ on the $\text{CH}$ carbons and two $\text{H}$ atoms on each $\text{CH}_2$, with extension bonds at both ends to show continuation.

Identify optical isomerism**
Focus on the $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}$ carbon. It is bonded to $\text{H}$, to $\text{CH}_3$, and to two different lengths of polymer chain on either side. With four different groups it is a chiral centre, so different arrangements around it are non superimposable mirror images.

Link structure to property**
Because these chiral centres can have different spatial configurations along the chain, poly(propene) can exist in isotactic, syndiotactic or atactic forms. That variation in 3D arrangement with the same connectivity is optical isomerism.

Final answer: Section: $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{-}$ with correct displayed groups.
Type: optical isomerism.
Explanation: the carbon attached to $\text{CH}_3$ has four different groups attached / is chiral.

hints: Think about why the strong non polar $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bonds in poly(propene) resist breakdown by microorganisms or water.
Think about what happens when a hydrocarbon polymer burns incompletely in landfill fires or incineration.
walkthrough:
Explain persistence in the environment**
Poly(propene) has long saturated hydrocarbon chains with strong $\text{C-C}$ bonds that bacteria and fungi cannot easily digest. It is non biodegradable, so it accumulates in landfill and takes many years to break down.

Explain the combustion problem**
Burning it as a disposal method needs very high temperature for complete combustion. Incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide, soot and other polluting gases, plus $\text{CO}_2$ which contributes to global warming. Sorting and recycling is also difficult and costly.

Final answer: 1. non-biodegradable / inert to decomposition, persists in landfill.
2. produces harmful / toxic gases such as $\text{CO}$ on combustion.

hints: Find the longest chain containing the $\text{C=C}$, number from the end nearest the double bond, then locate the two methyl branches on X.
walkthrough:
Name the skeleton of X**
Draw X out: $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_3$. The longest chain through the double bond has four carbons, so it is a butene. Number from the $\text{CH}_2$ end so the double bond starts at carbon 1, giving but-1-ene. There is a methyl on carbon 2 and a methyl on carbon 3, so the full name is 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.

hints: Compare the large peaks at $m/e$ 41 and 43 with the fragments each isomer can easily form, and note which peaks Y would give at 42 or 54 that are absent.
walkthrough:
Match fragments to structure**
Both X and Y are $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$, $M_r = 84$, so the molecular ion at 84 does not distinguish them. Look at fragmentation. X, $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_3$, cleaves readily to give $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5^+$ at $m/e$ 41 and $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$ at $m/e$ 43, both very intense in Fig. 4.2. Y, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$, would be expected to give strong fragments at $m/e$ 54 and 42, which are not significant. So the spectrum must be X.

Final answer: The spectrum is of X because peak at 41 is $\text{[CH}_2\text{=CCH}_3\text{]}^+$ / $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5^+$ or peak at 43 is $\text{[CH}_3\text{CHCH}_3\text{]}^+$ / $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$; Y would show significant peaks at 54 for $\text{[(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C]}^+$ or 42 for $\text{[(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C]}^+$ which are absent.

hints: Use that each carbon contributes about 1.1% to the $\text{[M+1]}^+$ intensity, so for a $\text{C}_6$ molecule multiply the M peak abundance by $6 \times 1.1 / 100$.
walkthrough:
Apply the $^{13}\text{C}$ rule**
The $\text{[M+1]}^+$ peak is mainly due to one $^{13}\text{C}$ in a molecule containing otherwise $^{12}\text{C}$. Natural abundance of $^{13}\text{C}$ is about 1.1% per carbon. For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$: $$\text{expected [M+1]}^+ = 34.7 \times \frac{6 \times 1.1}{100} = 34.7 \times 0.066 = 2.29$$ So the relative abundance is about 2.29 on the same scale.
Final answer: relative abundance $= 2.29$
